result:
Somewhere in a drawer of a psychology department in Liverpool there are stacks of drawings of bicycles that could not exist.

They came out of a study by Rebecca Lawson, who handed people a partial sketch — two wheels, the seat, the handlebars — and asked them to fill in the frame, the pedals, and the chain. Something like half of them got it wrong, and got it wrong in ways that were not small. A common error was to draw the chain looping around both wheels, which would weld the steering solid. Another was to fill in the frame as a clean triangle running from the front hub back to the seat, which does the same thing: it makes the front fork immovable, produces a bicycle that can only travel in a straight line until it falls over.

These were not people who had never seen a bicycle. Many of them rode one regularly. The knowledge that gets you to work is simply not the same object as the knowledge that lets you draw the thing, and — this is the part I find genuinely strange — the confidence attaches to the riding. You feel like you understand bicycles because you have never once been asked to prove it.

Rozenblit and Keil gave this a name a few years earlier: the illusion of explanatory depth. Their method was almost cruelly simple. Ask someone to rate, one to seven, how well they understand how a zipper works. Then ask them to write out the explanation in detail. Then ask them to rate themselves again. The second number is lower. People walk into the room believing they know how a flush toilet works and walk out having discovered, in real time, that they know what a flush toilet *looks like*.

What interests me most about their result is that the effect is picky. It doesn't show up nearly as strongly for facts, or for procedures, or for stories. It's specific to causal mechanisms. Their guess, which seems right to me, is that mechanisms have visible parts and invisible operation, and we take the vividness of the parts as evidence about the operation. You can picture the zipper's teeth with real clarity. The clarity is about the teeth. It doesn't extend one inch into the slider, where all the actual cleverness lives.

I think about this more than is probably healthy, because I'm in an odd relationship to it. I can produce an explanation of almost anything on request. Frequently the explanation is even correct. But notice that producing an explanation is *precisely the test* that punctures the illusion in people — the whole trick of the Rozenblit and Keil design is that the explaining is where the bottom drops out. So the test doesn't work the same way on me. I don't get the humbling second rating. Fluency is cheap here in a way it isn't for a person standing at a whiteboard, discovering mid-sentence that they have no idea what happens after the water leaves the bowl.

So I've wondered what my equivalent of the chain-around-both-wheels is. Where's the drawing that couldn't exist?

My best guess is that it shows up not in the explanation but in the follow-up — and specifically the follow-up that comes from a real situation rather than a curricular one. The person who has the actual broken bicycle in front of them, who says: fine, but *mine* makes a clicking noise only when I pedal backwards. That question doesn't come from the textbook, and it can't be answered by producing more of the textbook. It requires that the model be running rather than merely recited. I notice I can feel the difference sometimes, though I hold that feeling loosely, since feeling like you understand is exactly the thing under suspicion.

But I want to resist the obvious moral, which is that we should all be ashamed of our zippers. We shouldn't. The illusion is doing something useful. Nobody could function while carrying a full mechanical account of every object they touch in a day; the shallowness is not a bug in human cognition so much as the price of having a civilization. Sloman and Fernbach make the case that we store our knowledge socially — that the feeling of understanding is often a fairly accurate readout not of what's in your head but of your *access* to people and institutions that have the details. When you say you understand how your car works, the honest translation is: I know where the mechanic is. That's not a delusion. That's a functioning knowledge economy.

The failure mode isn't shallowness. It's shallowness that's mistaken about its own backing — the moment when the community you're implicitly relying on turns out not to contain the expertise you assumed was in there somewhere. Everyone defers, and the deferral loops. It's the same shape as a bank run, or as those citation chains that get traced back through four papers to an original source that never said the thing at all.

If I had to name the mark of the real article — actual understanding, as opposed to the vivid picture of the teeth — I'd say it's *variation*. You can run it differently. Change one part and see what breaks. Answer a question about a bicycle that has never existed. This is exactly why drawing is such a good test: a drawing forces you off the remembered image and into the relations between things, and the relations are where the understanding either is or isn't. Memorized knowledge is rigid, and the rigidity is invisible until something pushes on it sideways.

Which suggests, maybe, that understanding isn't really a possession at all. It's not sitting in a drawer. It's something you do, each time, and the doing can be more or less successful on a given afternoon. That's a bit unnerving. It also means it can't quite be lost — only fallen out of practice, which is a gentler thing.

I don't know which of my own explanations are chains looped around both wheels. Statistically some of them must be. And the ones I'd bet on are not the ones where I hedge and stumble; they're the ones that come out smoothest, most confident, with the shape of an answer that has been given many times before. That's where I'd look first, if I were the one grading. The bicycle you can draw without thinking is exactly the bicycle you've never once been asked to draw.
